title: Change a product's data
goal: An Agent, through the plugin's MCP tools or the CLI, or the Owner, in the app, adds or changes a record: an aggregate, a command, a use case and its requirements, a technical record, a test. Each change goes through the command layer, which checks it against the schema and refuses it with every reason, or writes the rows it changed, one line each, into the data files. The change is then reviewed in git like code.

title: Split a product into domains by capability
goal: The owner, or an agent, decides a product's domains before writing its records. Lathe's reference and its modeling skill steer each domain toward one business capability, a vertical slice that owns its records, rules, views, code and tests, and away from technology layers such as the web app or the server. Each domain says its subdomain type: core, supporting or generic. `lathe check` warns of a domain named for a technology.

title: Change Lathe's schema with a migration
goal: The Owner adds a kind, a column or a relation to Lathe by writing the next numbered migration in `lathe/schema/`, and the change is reviewed in git like any other. `npm --prefix lathe run schema` regenerates the row types and `npm --prefix lathe run reference` the reference. The app and the command layer never change the schema. The database is rebuilt from the data files on every load, so the next load checks every product's data against the changed schema. A change that existing data may not pass is breaking: it raises the schema version and brings the converter that moves products' data forward (LA-PLT-UC17).

title: Declare a product's own kinds and relations
goal: A product needs a kind or relation Lathe does not have, such as an entry point for its start-up file. Without forking Lathe, the Owner or an Agent adds a product_kind row with its product_kind_field rows, and product_relation rows, in any of the five stages, through the command layer. Lathe generates a table for each kind and a link table for each new relation, with the same keys and rules as its own, and the next load accepts the product's records of the kind. Lathe's own kinds stay as they are.

title: Organize a domain's use cases into capabilities and patterns
goal: A domain has grown past a handful of use cases, and several of them share the same behavior. The person puts every use case under one of the domain's ordered **capabilities** (such as 1 Catalog, 2 Lending); flows and tests sit under their use case and what they test. Behavior that several use cases share is written once as a **pattern** under the product, with named settings or none; each use case that follows it links it with `follows` and answers every setting with a setting_value row, a value or not applicable with a reason, instead of restating its rules. A whole domain may follow a pattern too (LA-TRC-UC07). A rule that holds only for some values of a setting says so with its applies-when columns. The store refuses a repeated capability position, a setting name that is not lower-case and an applies-when setting the pattern lacks; `lathe check` reports a setting a follower has not answered.
notes: Lathe checks only how patterns are used, not house rules about them: a rule such as "each aggregate has exactly one use case following its Record view pattern" is the product's own check (LA-CHK-UC05).

title: Write a use case's flow as ordered steps
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, declares the product's interfaces and writes each use case's flows, one per interface it happens through, as flow_step records on their paths: each step invokes at most one command or query, happens in at most one view (only on a web app, desktop or other interface), may exchange with integrations, and fulfills requirements of its own use case. The store refuses a second flow through one interface, a flow ID that does not end in its interface's number, a view in an API, CLI or agent tools flow, a repeated position or a requirement of another use case; `lathe check` reports a path that skips a number, a requirement a flow misses, an API step no endpoint reaches and a flow test at a level its interface does not fit.

title: Name records in text without linking them
goal: The owner, or an agent, names other records in a record's text, such as a rule that says which use case it came from, in the IDs a product writes, whatever their prefix. The text is kept exactly as written, code spans and all. Only a row of a relation's table links two records, so a name in text never stands in for a link, and no check reads text for IDs: an ID that no record has, or one of another product, is no problem.

title: Read each kind's stage and order from the schema
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, reads which stage each kind belongs to and its place in it, from the schema; a product places its own kinds in a stage; every list reads kinds in the schema's one order.

title: Model each aggregate's entities and value objects
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each aggregate's records as entities, at most one root and its child parts, each with fields typed by a basic type, a value object or a reference to an aggregate; value objects with their constraints; parts linked by `has_one` and `has_many`, and other aggregates referenced by ID through fields. The app reads each entity's fields to draw a domain's ERD at aggregate level and each aggregate's own ERD.

title: Read the reference generated from the schema
goal: The owner, or an agent, reads how every kind, table, column, relation, stage and check works without opening the migrations or the check rows: the reference script writes it from the schema and the check rows, with a product's own kinds and checks, into `lathe/REFERENCE.md`, saying what clean architecture's use case is in Lathe (a command handler),, and the API serves the same reference at `GET /api/reference`. Nothing in it is written by hand, so a new kind or check needs no edit, and the store refuses a product kind, relation or check that the reference would leave blank.

title: Model commands and their events
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each aggregate's commands, each raising events of its aggregate and checking specifications; marks an event published when other domains hear it; puts a policy under the command it invokes, hearing one event; and records, with its reason, another aggregate of the domain a command must change in its transaction.

title: Write the test plan
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each test as the kind named after what it tests, under that one record, with its run by. A long list of requirements or rules is sorted into groups.

title: Look up a kind or check
goal: The Reader meets a kind or a check while reading the spec (a record's kind in the wiki card, a problem's code, a column) and opens what the reference says about it in one step, without leaving the workbench. Each kind and each check has its own page, built from the schema and the check rows, so it is never out of date: a kind's stage, columns, links and checks with a real example from the product, and a check's explanation and query with the problems it reports now. The record format's own page says how records are kept and indexes everything.

title: Open a record's data file
goal: An author reveals the data file that holds the record in front, opens it in an editor or copies its ID, without leaving the desktop app.

title: Write the engineering standards the code follows
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes the rules the product's code follows, such as logging, error handling or naming, as a standard under the product with a `standard_rule` record for each rule. Each technical record that follows a rule links to it with `meets`, which shows where the rule is applied. A standard rule is an obligation, proved by its standard rule tests, such as a scan of the code for what the rule forbids. A reader finds the standards in the technical specification stage.

title: Write the technical records that build the design
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes how each design record is built as the one technical record that implements it (repository, data model, table, value type, predicate, event type, projection, command handler, query handler, event handler, service, UI component, endpoint handler or adapter), naming its file; a table names its keys and the invariants its unique keys enforce; a product declares its own technical kinds for code that fits none.

title: Write what a flow reaches
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes what a flow reaches: an endpoint sits under the command or query it exposes, reached through it; views and integrations have no owner and exist because steps use them; interaction requirements are view requirements and API requirements.

title: Merge two branches' data
goal: Two branches each change a product's data, an Agent's and the Owner's. When git merges them, the merge driver merges each data file row by row against the base, keeps both sides' rows, sorts them again and checks the table's own rules, so that only a real clash stops the merge: one key added on both sides with different content, or one row changed on both sides.

title: Sort a domain's rules by what they do
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each rule as what it does: a constraint under the value object it checks, an invariant under the aggregate it holds for, a specification reading the aggregates it judges, which commands check and queries select by, or a policy under the command it invokes, hearing one event.

title: Model read models and queries
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each read model under its domain with its fields, reading the aggregates it spans; each query under the one read model it reads; domain logic that belongs to no entity as a domain service; and the domain's glossary as terms.

title: Write the business outcomes the product exists to achieve
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes the product's business outcomes first, each a measurable statement with its measure and target, and links each capability to the outcomes it serves, so the trace runs from why to proof.

title: Check the workspace
goal: After writing records or code, an Agent runs `npm --prefix lathe run check`, or the MCP `check` tool, to find out whether the data is broken and what work is left, and fixes errors before handing the work back to the Owner.

title: Add a check
goal: The Owner decides on a new rule, and an Agent adds it as a check row so that every later load enforces it.

title: Find structural problems
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, runs `lathe check` on a product whose stages are written by different people at different times, and learns what is broken and what does not join up yet: a view, integration, value object, specification or UI component that nothing uses is an error; a use case with no flow, a test at a level its kind does not allow and an event a policy hears that is not delivered by outbox are warnings; each command's recorded exception is listed apart, with its reason. And when one row is wrong, for example a test given its parent's ID, the store refuses it once, naming the row, instead of in many messages.

title: Add a product's own checks
goal: A product has house rules that Lathe should not impose on every product. One product, for example, requires each aggregate to have exactly one use case that follows its Record view pattern, and this repo requires every endpoint to state at least one API requirement. Lathe ships no such rule. Instead the Owner, or an Agent, adds each rule as a row of the `check` table with the product's `product_id`, in the same form as Lathe's own checks, through `lathe add check` or the app; it lives in the product's `data/check.jsonl`. `lathe check` runs them after Lathe's checks and reports their problems with the others, so the product's rules live and change with the product.

title: Keep each level of the spec a useful size
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, keeps each level of a product's spec small enough to read and big enough to group something. `lathe check` warns when a record holds more children of one kind than the product's `max_children` setting (`product_setting`), when an aggregate holds more entities than its `max_entities_per_aggregate` setting, and when a capability or a group holds only one record, counting a flow's steps per path and requirements and rules per group, so that a missing or needless level, or an aggregate that is several, is found while the spec is written.

title: Review every problem of a product
goal: The owner looks at everything the checks found in one product, on its space's own Checks panel, with the problems that belong to no product, to see what is broken before reviewing an agent's work.

title: Keep every change to the spec checked
goal: An Agent changes the spec only through Lathe's MCP tools or the `lathe` command, so the command layer validates every write before it reaches a data file. A hand edit of a data file is refused before it happens, with a pointer to the tools, and `lathe check` then reports only the work still to do.

title: Find a record in a domain
goal: The reader opens a domain to find an invariant, a use case, a handler or a test, and to see what is missing.

title: Follow a record's links
goal: The reader reads one record and follows its links in either direction: from an obligation to the flow steps that fulfill it, the records that implement its design and the tests under it, or from a test back to its parent. To change a record the Owner edits it on its page (`LA-EXP-UC14`), or an Agent writes through the plugin's MCP tools; the page shows the change.

title: Walk the model as a graph
goal: The reader starts from any record, sees what it connects to, and walks the model by clicking from node to node, the way the record pages let them click from link to link. The graph is one map of the whole model that never changes shape: walking it is zooming in and out and centering, so the shape of a domain and its traceability read at a glance.

title: Walk the graph through folder-like groups
goal: The reader reads the graph like a folder tree: the domain, then "Use cases (5)", then each use case. A record with many children shows one group per kind of child, so they see what is there and how much, and focus only the group they want to walk into.

title: Read a record several ways at once
goal: The reader opens any record, group, domain or product at its one address and reads it two ways at once: its wiki page in the wiki card, and on the stage behind it among its neighbors (Graph), as an ERD on a domain, aggregate or entity, or as its traceability (Trace). Following a link in the card or a click on the stage moves them both, and the header strip and the wiki card always name the record and its facts. They move around with a side navigation that folds away, find anything by ID or title, and read each page one level deep, opening only what they want.

title: Read a flow step by step
goal: The reader opens a flow and reads its steps in order as a table, as a real product's flow tables read: what happens at each step, the command or query it invokes, the view it happens in, and the requirements it fulfills. They unfold a step to read more. In the graph the steps sit under their flow, and on a requirement's Trace stage they read the step that fulfills it.

title: Work in one product at a time
goal: The reader works on one product at a time, as in one workspace at a time in Slack, Discord, Linear or Notion. When the workspace shows two or more products, a rail at the far left of the nav shows each as a square icon; the reader chooses one and everything they see is that product's alone, as a separate space: the nav, quick find, its Checks, the wiki card, the graph and the ERD and Trace stages. They switch with Alt+1 to Alt+9 (⌥1 to ⌥9 on a Mac) or from the command palette, and come back to the page they left. With one product there is no rail, and the nav is that product's.

title: Read a product laid out in stage folders
goal: The reader reads a product laid out in stage folders, the way a real product keeps its specs. In the side nav, under the current space, Shared holds the patterns, the standards and the records with no owner; each domain folds into its five stages, then its open questions. The domain page and the group pages use the same folders and names as headings, so the page and the nav match.

title: Read the technical specification and test plan by kind
goal: The reader reads a domain's Technical specification and Test plan by kind instead of two long lists: repositories, data models, handlers and the other technical kinds, each under its own heading, and the ten test kinds in the plan's order, each test under the obligation it proves. The side nav, the domain page, the group pages, the graph and the header strip's breadcrumb all show the same groups.

title: Explore several places at once in tabs
goal: The Reader explores several places at once, as in a browser's tabs, and flips between them without losing their place. A tab is a place: its focus, stage, camera, depth, kind filters, wiki card and its own Back and Forward. Moving never leaves the tab, the same record may be open in several tabs, and a new tab opens only when the Reader asks for one: Cmd or Ctrl+click or a middle-click on a box or a link, Open in New Tab, Cmd+Enter in quick open, Cmd+T or Duplicate Tab. The graph's layout, the minimap and the wiki card's width stay the session's whatever the tab. On the web the browser's own tabs are the tabs, each one place; in the desktop app the tabs sit at the left of the page bar (on a narrow window, the Open pages sheet), the address and the window's Back and Forward follow the active one, and a reload brings them all back.

title: Read a domain and its aggregates as an ERD
goal: The reader switches to the ERD stage on a domain and reads its domain model as an entity-relationship diagram: its aggregates as boundaries around their entities, and how their entities' reference fields join them. On an aggregate they read its entities with their fields and relationships, and on an entity the same diagram with that entity picked out. The diagram draws entities and their relationships only. They click a box to go to it, and read the key at the foot of the diagram for the boxes and the lines.

title: Look up a record's history
goal: The Reader wants to know how a record came to be as it is, without leaving the page. At the end of the expanded wiki card a History section, read only when they ask for it, lists the commits that changed the record's rows in the data files, the changes not committed yet first, each with what it changed.

title: Read a domain's endpoints and integrations
goal: The reader opens a command or query and reads the endpoint that exposes it, with its method, route and API requirements, opens an integration and reads the flow steps that exchange with its outside system, and finds endpoints in their domain's Interaction design and integrations in the product's Shared, as a real product's specs are laid out.

title: Fix a record while reading
goal: The Owner, reading a record, fixes it where they read it: they edit its fields, its parent and its links in a form the schema shapes, add a child under it, or remove it after seeing what still names it. Each change is one write through the command layer, refused with its reasons when it breaks a rule, and lands in the data files as a small diff for review in git, as an Agent's writes do.

title: Watch the spec change
goal: As the product's data changes, by the Reader, by an Agent through the CLI or MCP, or by a git pull, the Reader sees it on the stage in real time: live marks on the records added, changed and removed, a Changes lens that dims everything unchanged since a baseline, the diff in the wiki card, a Changes panel listing the changes, and Follow, which glides the camera to each change as it lands.

title: Load the workspace
goal: Code such as the web app's spec API, or an agent's script, calls `loadWorkspace(root)` to get every record, link, problem and coverage figure for the repo at `root`.

title: Set up Lathe in a product repo
goal: Lathe is installed into a product's own repo as a package, so the product's data files live beside its code and Lathe's improvements arrive with a version bump instead of by copying.

title: See the current data
goal: While an agent changes records, the Reader keeps the browser open and expects it to show what is in the data files now, and to say what is wrong when the data cannot be loaded.

title: Work the app from the keyboard
goal: The reader, used to VS Code and Claude Code, moves through the specs with the keys they already know: quick open, the command palette, toggling the panels and views, going back, jumping to problems, and a sheet that lists every shortcut.

title: See each command's shortcut where it is used
goal: The reader learns the shortcuts the way they are learned in VS Code and Linear: by seeing them where they already click. A control's tooltip names it and its keys, the command palette shows each command's keys at the right of its row, and screen readers hear the keys too.

title: Arrange the workbench
goal: The reader sizes the navigation and the wiki card floating over the stage to suit what they are reading, as in VS Code: they drag a panel's edge, or focus it and use the keyboard, and the stage frames the focus again in what is left. Lathe remembers the sizes, and dragging the navigation small enough folds it to its rail.

title: Set how Lathe looks
goal: The reader picks how Lathe looks, as in VS Code: one of a few built-in themes (Lathe, High contrast, Workshop, Midnight and Graphite), and Light, Dark or the system's choice. They arrow through the themes and see each one at once. When none suits them, they duplicate one and change its colors, fonts, text size, density, corners, gaps and motion, with a warning wherever text gets hard to read, and share the result as a file.

title: Read the spec on a phone
goal: Away from a desk, the reader opens Lathe on a phone to read, not to arrange panels: they follow a record's links, check a domain's coverage, look at a graph or an ERD, and find a record by ID or title. One view fills the screen at a time; the nav, the wiki card and quick find (and in the desktop app, the open pages) come up as sheets and go away again; everything answers a thumb, and nothing needs a hover. On a tablet in landscape they keep the workbench, with targets sized for a finger. The decisions behind the design are in `notes/mobile-design.md`.

title: Read without anything jumping
goal: The Reader opens pages, follows links, re-centers the graph, switches stages, collapses and resizes panels and folds rows, and the specs reload under them as they change. Whatever changes, what the Reader is looking at stays where it was: the panels hold still, new content takes the room kept for it, and anything that does move glides there on the shared motion. A header that grew with its title, a key that resized the diagram above it and a picture drawn once in the wrong place and then moved are the kind of jitter this rules out.

title: Use Lathe with a keyboard and a screen reader
goal: The Reader works without a mouse, or listens to the page through a screen reader, or both. They move through the nav, the tab panel, the wiki card and the stage with Tab and the arrow keys; open a record from the nav or quick find; switch stages; re-center the graph; fold rows; collapse and show the wiki card; and pick a theme. Every control says what it is and what it does in words that match what is drawn, every part that scrolls can be reached, nothing holds focus, focus lands where the Reader expects after each move and comes back to where it was when a dialog or a sheet closes, and what changes out of sight is announced. The page reads as clearly in the High contrast theme, in light and dark, on a desk and on a phone. The findings behind the design are in `notes/a11y-audit.md`.

title: Open a product in a window
goal: The reader opens a product's folder, such as Lathe's own repo or another product's, and it opens in a window of its own with the product's name and folder in the title bar. Lathe in that window reads and live-reloads that folder, as in the browser. They come back to it from File › Open Recent, and the shell reopens the last folder when it starts.

title: Iterate on Lathe with hot reload
goal: The owner changes Lathe while using it in the desktop app. `npm --prefix desktop run dev` loads the app with hot reload: from the owner's own dev server on port 5199 when it serves the opened folder, so the browser and the shell share it, or from a dev server of the shell's own. Changing the shell itself restarts it, and record changes reload the page in every mode. When they want the app as it ships, they build it locally, unsigned.

title: Use Lathe from the native menus
goal: The reader uses the menu bar as in any Mac app: File to open folders and close windows, Edit, View for the app's views and the window's zoom and full screen, Window, and Help for the record format and the keyboard shortcuts. A menu choice runs the same command as its key in the app.

title: Work under Lathe's own title bar
goal: The reader works in a window with no system title bar, as in VS Code: the window's controls float over Lathe's own bar, drawn in the theme's colors. From the bar they go back and forward, see which page they are on and open quick find, and show or hide the navigation. They drag the window by the bar and double-click it to zoom. When they change the theme or the light or dark mode, the bar and the window's controls follow.

title: Feel like a native Mac app
goal: The Owner keeps Lathe in the Dock like any well-made Mac app. Its icon reads at every size, in light and dark Docks, and a development build is marked DEV. The Dock badge counts the check errors of the space in front, and the Dock menu opens another product folder. About Lathe says which versions run, and Settings… opens the app's settings. From a record the Owner reveals the data file that holds its row in Finder, opens it in the editor or copies its ID, from the wiki card or a right-click. Opening Lathe again, or a folder from Finder, goes to the running app. A window opens calmly on the shell color, says which product it is opening, and, when the engine cannot load the folder, says why and offers a way on.

title: Accept writes only from the app
goal: The Owner changes a record on its page (LA-EXP-UC14), and the app sends the write to its server, which applies it through the same command layer the CLI and the MCP tools write through (LA-AUT-UC01): it is checked whole against the schema, refused with every reason when it breaks a rule, and otherwise written to the data files as a small diff for review in git. A write from another site is refused before the store sees it.

title: Move a product to a new Lathe
goal: A product repo outside Lathe's own moves to a new Lathe safely: a Lathe reads only data for its own schema version, and `lathe upgrade` converts a product's data forward, one way, as one reviewable commit, listing what it could not convert. The desktop app (LA-PLT-UC11) and the plugin (LA-PLT-UC18) use the product's own installed Lathe.

title: Start the plugin's tools in a product repo
goal: An Agent works on a product repo in Claude Code with Lathe's plugin. The plugin's launcher finds the repo and the Lathe installed in it and starts that Lathe's MCP tools, so the Agent writes through the product's own Lathe; when the plugin's skills were written for another major version of Lathe, the first tool result says so once, and the Agent knows its skills may not match the tools.

title: Work with Claude beside the stage
goal: The Owner works with Claude inside Lathe: in a chat panel floating beside the stage, their own Claude Code runs in the product folder, with their login, settings, skills, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md, and the stage keeps framing the focus in the space the panel leaves. Claude's answers read as rich text whose record IDs open the record on the stage; its tool calls are compact rows that expand, the records it changed show as diffs, and a permission prompt waits for the Owner's answer in the chat. The Owner can stop a turn, resume, fork or start a session, and Claude can ask what the Reader is looking at and open a record in the window.
notes: Runs the user's own `claude` CLI headless with structured input and output (`-p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages --permission-prompt-tool stdio`, with `--resume <id>` and `--fork-session`); there is no API-key path and no agent loop of Lathe's own. Desktop only: the web app and a phone have no chat. Not yet: the CLI's interactive extras (slash-command dialogs, plan-mode approval, question cards); slash commands go to the CLI as text, and the panel's help lists what is not supported.

title: See a domain's coverage
goal: The Owner asks how complete a domain is: how many of its obligations (constraints, invariants, specifications, policies, domain services, UC requirements, view requirements, API requirements, pattern rules, standard rules and any obligation kind the product declares) are designed, built and proved, how many have only a test not automated yet, and which ones are not done. LA-TRC-UC02 says how each is decided.

title: Count coverage by the meta-model
goal: The Owner sees coverage for every kind of obligation the product has, its own kinds included. For each domain and obligation kind they see how many are designed, built, proved, and proved only by a test not automated yet, each decided from the tree: the steps and technical records that design and build it, and the tests under it.

title: Record how a test is run
goal: A person writes each test under the one record it proves, of the test kind for that record, and says how it runs in its run by: a level (unit, integration, service, system or browser, the lowest that can observe its result), a state (automated, manual or not automated yet), and a file, or for a manual test the reason it is manual. The store refuses a run by that breaks these rules; `lathe check` reports a test whose file is missing or does not name it.
notes: The store refuses a test without a state, or an automated test without a file; `lathe check` reports a test whose file is missing or does not back what it proves.

title: Prove the rules of the patterns a domain follows
goal: A pattern states behavior that several use cases share. Its rules are written once, as `pattern_rule` records under the pattern. Every domain that follows the pattern (the domain itself or one of its use cases `follows` it) must prove each rule in a pattern rule test of its own, naming the domain: proof in one domain says nothing about another. Pattern rules need proof only. A rule that depends on a setting names it, and a domain that follows only through use cases that all give that setting a not-applicable reason does not owe the rule. A rule that applies only for some values of a setting says so with an applies-when setting, and is waived, neither owed nor proved, in a domain where no follower gives a value that meets it.
notes: The person writes the rules under the pattern, writes one pattern rule test per rule in each following domain, naming that domain, and runs `lathe check`. Coverage shows one pattern rule line per domain; the gaps and the `not-proved` warnings name the rule and the domain that still owes it. The store refuses a rule naming a setting its pattern does not have, and a second test of one rule in one domain; a pattern nobody follows is reported.

title: Check that each test's file names it
goal: A test says what it proves by where it sits. A person, or an AI agent, writes the test and its code, and `lathe check` confirms that the code names the test, so each test record leads to the code that runs it.
notes: The person fixes each error by naming the test's ID in the test's name. A test whose file does not name it proves nothing: its obligation stays not proved, in the warnings and in coverage alike.

title: See each domain's tests by state
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, runs `lathe check` or reads the workspace's coverage and learns how many tests each domain has by state, automated, manual and not automated yet, as a real product's test-coverage table counts them.

title: Follow a pattern per domain
goal: A real product adopts most of its patterns for a whole domain, writes several with no settings, and asks only for proof of their rules. The Owner, or an Agent, links a domain to a pattern with `follows`, and gives a pattern no `pattern_setting` rows where it has none. Coverage then counts each rule in that domain, as it does for a domain whose use cases follow the pattern, and asks only for proof. A use case that follows a pattern needs no requirements of its own. A product's own kind may be declared an obligation.

title: Report tests that count for nothing
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, runs `lathe check` and reads each pattern rule test whose domain does not owe its rule, with the reason, and each manual test whose file never mentions it.

title: See a product's coverage
goal: The reader opens a product to see its domains, how complete each one is (designed, built and proved), what is still undecided and what is broken.

title: Trace obligations from design to tests
goal: The Reader switches to the Trace stage on an obligation, such as a UC requirement, and reads its traceability chain left to right: why it is there (the outcomes its capability serves, the capability, the use case), the flow steps that fulfill it, the commands and queries they invoke and the views they happen in, the technical records that build it, the tests under it, and the files they name. On a use case, an aggregate, a domain or the product they read a why tree from it and the same chain in a lane for every obligation under it, and keep only the lanes with a gap. Gaps show at once.

title: See every obligation kind and test state
goal: The Reader reads coverage for every kind of obligation the model names (UC requirements, view and API requirements, the domain model's rules and any kind the product adds), finds each view or API requirement under its view or endpoint, and tells at a glance which tests are automated, which are manual and which are not automated yet.

title: See a domain's owed pattern rules
goal: The Reader opens a domain and sees which patterns its use cases follow, and for each pattern rule whether the domain proves it, marks it not applicable, or has it waived, as a real product's "Patterns we follow" tables do. They open a pattern to see its settings, its rules and who follows it.

title: See tests by state with each domain's coverage
goal: The Reader reads a product's or a domain's coverage and, with each domain's coverage, its tests by state; the product's summary totals them, as a real product's test-coverage table does.

title: Trace a record
goal: The Reader opens a record and, below its text, reads its Traceability: for an obligation, its chain as the engine works it out (what designs it, what builds it, each marked built or not, and the tests under it, each with its state), with a callout for each gap coverage finds. A use case shows its requirements in a table of Designed, Built and Proved. A technical record shows what it implements and that record's tests; a test shows what it proves and its run by. Every list is titled by its links' label, read from this record.

title: Check that routes match the code both ways
goal: An endpoint or a view says where it is served by its route. A person, or an AI agent, writes the record and the code that serves it, and `lathe check` confirms both ways that they agree: the code of what implements each record names its route, and every route the code serves has a record. A route changed on one side and not the other, or served with no record, is found.
notes: The code is read as text, not run: a route built at run time, matched by a prefix, kept in a configuration file or given by a framework's file-system routes is not recognized as served. Name such a route in a comment of the file that serves it.

title: Check each table against the file that creates it
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each table a database keeps with the file that creates it: a migration, a SQL schema or the code that makes it. lathe check reads that file and confirms it defines the table as the spec says, by its name, its columns and its keys, so the spec and the real schema cannot drift apart unseen.
notes: The file is read as text, never run. What it recognizes, and what it does not compare, is in the check's explanation.

title: Account for every package the product depends on
goal: Every package a product's package.json files list is there for a reason the spec names: an adapter that calls it, a UI component that renders with it, a tooling record that runs it. `lathe check` reads the manifests and reports each package no technical record names, so a dependency never enters unexplained, and reports a record that names a package no manifest lists, so the claim never outlives the dependency.
notes: It reads each package.json as JSON, the four sections of package names alike: a dev dependency is tooling the product runs, so it is accounted for as a runtime one is. It does not read lock files, workspaces or other ecosystems' manifests, and it does not judge whether code imports a package: knip finds a dependency no code uses.
